items.title: kubelet: containers that fail before ever running don't get exponential CrashLoopBackOff treatment
items.text:
### What happened?

When `startContainer` fails before the container ever reaches a running state — e.g. `CreateContainer` is rejected by the CRI because a resource limit (such as memory) is below the runtime's floor, or a pre-create/pre-start hook fails , no container status is ever recorded for that attempt.

`kubeGenericRuntimeManager.doBackOff` decides whether to apply `CrashLoopBackOff` by looking for an *exited* container status in `podStatus.ContainerStatuses`. Since these pre-run failures never produce a container status, `doBackOff` never finds one to back off against.

The pod is still retried (the pod-worker's flat ~10s backoff on `SyncPod` errors still applies , see `backOffPeriod` in `pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go`), but these container-start failures never get the *exponential* backoff or the `CrashLoopBackOff` reason/event that other persistently-failing containers get once they've run and exited at least once. This is inconsistent: two containers that both fail forever are treated differently depending on whether the failure happened before or after the container briefly started.



### What did you expect to happen?

Containers that repeatedly fail to start , even before ever reaching a running state — should get the same exponential backoff escalation (up to the standard cap) and `CrashLoopBackOff` status/event reporting as containers that repeatedly exit after starting.



### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Pod with a container whose resource request/limit is set below what the container runtime enforces as a floor (e.g. a memory limit below the runtime's minimum).
2. Observe that `CreateContainer` is rejected on every retry.
3. Observe that kubelet retries at a flat ~10s cadence indefinitely, without back-off

items.title: Evented PLEG: kubelet panics under host pressure
items.text:
### What happened?

While testing evented PLEG locally, I encountered an issue where the kubelet panics when pods are created rapidly. The panic produces the following logs:
```
E0608 18:40:24.994902 1066258 evented.go:365] "Evented PLEG: Get cache" err="rpc error: code = DeadlineExceeded desc = context deadline exceeded" podID="7316163d-1d4e-484e-9943-434fda242f36"
panic: send on closed channel

goroutine 451 [running]:
k8s.io/cri-client/pkg.(*remoteRuntimeService).GetContainerEvents(0xc0004cdce0, {0x34abd70, 0x5038e40}, 0xc00045d6c0, 0x3158798)
	k8s.io/cri-client/pkg/remote_runtime.go:848 +0x1b4
k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/pleg.(*EventedPLEG).watchEventsChannel.func1()
	k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/pleg/evented.go:199 +0x82
created by k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/pleg.(*EventedPLEG).watchEventsChannel in goroutine 440
	k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/pleg/evented.go:184 +0xae
```
This is not a typical issue. The root cause appears to be a synchronization problem between goroutine lifecycles and channel lifecycles, resulting in attempts to send data to a closed channel. One possible solution might involve introducing a cancellable context or notifying producers when the channel is closed to prevent sending messages to a closed channel.

### What did you expect to happen?

kubelet does not panic.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

On a node with limited resources (4-core CPU, 8GB RAM), with the EventedPLEG feature gate enabled, rapidly create a large number of pods (exceeding 600).

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

items.title: Pods stuck in ImagePullBackOff hold their resource requests on the node indefinitely, with no way to reclaim the capacity
items.text:
### What would you like to be added?

A supported way to bound how long a Pod may sit in `ImagePullBackOff` before it becomes terminal, so that the node capacity its resource requests reserve is released. For example a kubelet-level `imagePullBackOffDeadline` (or an equivalent pod-level field): once exceeded, kubelet fails the Pod (`status.phase: Failed`) instead of retrying the pull forever, and the scheduler stops charging its requests to the node.

### Why is this needed?

A Pod in `ImagePullBackOff` is already **bound** (`spec.nodeName` is set) and **non-terminal** (`status.phase: Pending`). kube-scheduler charges the requests of every bound Pod against the node's allocatable, and the only predicate anywhere in that path is "does it have a node name":

- [`pkg/scheduler/eventhandlers.go#L452-L454`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.3/pkg/scheduler/eventhandlers.go#L452-L454) — `assignedPod()` is `len(pod.Spec.NodeName) != 0`
- [`pkg/scheduler/eventhandlers.go#L136-L138`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.3/pkg/scheduler/eventhandlers.go#L136-L138) — assigned Pods go to the scheduler cache, unassigned ones to the scheduling queue
- [`pkg/scheduler/backend/cache/cache.go#L437-L448`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.3/pkg/scheduler/backend/cache/cache.go#L437-L448) — `addPod()` → `n.info.AddPod(pod)`
- [`pkg/scheduler/framework/types.go#L439-L452`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.36.3/pkg/scheduler/framework/types.go#L439-L452) — `NodeInfo.update()` → `n.Requested.MilliCPU += ...`

items.title: Parallel image pull should pull unique images only once
items.text:
### What would you like to be added?

Creating large amount of pods that all use the same image causes the kubelet to start pull per each pod, when parallel pull is enabled. This causes the reigstry QPS to be used, slowing down other pods with other images and also wastes the bandwidth for downloading the same images multiple times.

If same image is being already downloaded in parallel, other pods should just wait for it, not starting new download and not using up registry QPS. 

### Why is this needed?

We have use case where we start large number (500+) pods at the same time where many pods gets scheduled on single node (100+), and most pods have same init container with the same image (given the image on the container is provided with full SHA digest).

This causes lot of bandwidth on the node to be used during the startup of those pods, and also some pods are delayed due to `ImagePullBackoff` caused by `pull QPS exceeded`.

items.title: `StatefulSet` update stuck at the previous error
items.text:
### What happened?

When update a `StatefulSet` image, if the pod get error like `ErrImagePull/ImagePullBackOff`, then if update the `StatefulSet` image again with a valid image, then the sts pod will stuck at the previous error, unless delete the error pod manually will trigger the new image rolling update.

Demo yaml to reproduce:
vim demo-sts.yaml
```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: nginx-sts
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  serviceName: nginx
  replicas: 3
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.7.9
```
1). `kubectl apply -f demo-sts.yaml`, will see 3 pods running normally.
```
k get po
NAME          READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
nginx-sts-0   1/1     Running   0          10s
nginx-sts-1   1/1     Running   0          6s
nginx-sts-2   1/1     Running   0          5s
```
2). `kubectl edit sts nginx-sts` with a invalid image tag `nginx:1.7.9-a`, then will see:
```
k get po
NAME          READY   STATUS         RESTARTS   AGE
nginx-sts-0   1/1     Running        0          109s
nginx-sts-1   1/1     Running        0          105s
nginx-sts-2   0/1     ErrImagePull   0          4s
```
3). `kubectl edit sts nginx-sts` again with a valid image tag `nginx:1.8.1`, then will see the error pod will always stuck at the previous error, no rolling update.
```
k get po
NAME          READY   STATUS         RESTARTS   AGE
nginx-sts-0   1/1     Running        0          7m6s
nginx-sts-1   1/1     Running        0          7m2s
nginx-sts-2   0/1     ErrImagePull   0          3m12s
```
4). `k delete po nginx-sts-2` delete the error pod manually will trigger the new image rolling update to finish.

items.title: machine-readable scheduling failure diagnostics for unscheduled Pods
items.text:
### What would you like to be added?

I would like to discuss whether Kubernetes should expose more structured, machine-readable scheduling failure diagnostics for Pods that cannot be scheduled.

Today, kube-scheduler reports scheduling failures through `FailedScheduling` Events and the `PodScheduled` condition. However, the detailed causes are primarily encoded in human-readable messages, for example:

```text
0/3 nodes are available: 1 Insufficient cpu, 2 node(s) had untolerated taint ...
```

This is useful for humans, but difficult for automation and troubleshooting tools to consume reliably without parsing message strings.

This issue is intended to start a discussion before drafting a KEP. I understand that feature requests are unlikely to make progress as issues alone, and I plan to engage with SIG Scheduling on Slack and consider a KEP if the problem space is considered worth pursuing.

A possible direction could be to expose stable scheduling failure categories, for example:

```yaml
status:
  schedulingDiagnostics:
    result: Unschedulable
    reasonCodes:
    - InsufficientCPU
    - TaintMismatch
    failedPlugins:
    - NodeResourcesFit
    - TaintToleration
```

This is only an illustrative example. I am not proposing a final API shape in this issue.

Initial scope could be:

preserve the existing FailedScheduling Events
preserve the existing PodScheduled condition behavior
avoid changing scheduling decisions
avoid exposing per-node detailed failure data by default
define a generic diagnostics format that scheduler plugins could contribute to
avoid solving feature-specific diagnostics for Gang Scheduling, DRA, or preemption in the first step

Non-goals:

change scheduling semantics
introduce a new scheduling policy
replace existing Events

items.title: `Pod didn't trigger scale-up` should specify needs
items.text:
### What happened?

> Pod didn't trigger scale-up: 9 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector, 3 Insufficient cpu, 3 node(s) had untolerated taint(s), 3 in backoff after failed scale-up

### What did you expect to happen?

- When `cpu` is insufficient, the event should include the required cpu (note that this is often the sum of a number of containers, and thus something that kubernetes calculated but not something easily seen when looking at a pod)
- When `memory` is insufficient, the event should include the required memory (note that this is often the sum of a number of containers, and thus something that kubernetes calculated but not something easily seen when looking at a pod)
- When `taint` is untolerated, if there is only one (or maybe two), list it
- When `node affinity`/`node selector` isn't matched and there is only one (or maybe two), list it

items.title: scheduler: pods blocked by namespaceSelector podAffinity are not requeued on matching pod add or namespace label change
items.text:
### What happened?

A pod whose only scheduling blocker is a required podAffinity term with a namespaceSelector stays Pending with no new scheduling attempt after a cluster change that makes it schedulable:

- an assigned pod matching the term labelSelector appears in a namespace whose labels match the namespaceSelector (assigned pod add), or
- labels are added to a namespace so that an existing assigned pod now matches the namespaceSelector.

The pod is only retried by the periodic unschedulable pods sweep (`--pod-max-in-unschedulable-pods-duration`, default 5m, deprecated), and it schedules successfully on the first attempt after the sweep.

A control with the same affinity term but without namespaceSelector (matching a pod in the same namespace) is requeued and scheduled within about 10s of the matching pod being added.

### What did you expect to happen?

The pod should be requeued when an assigned pod that satisfies the affinity term, including namespaceSelector evaluation, is added, consistent with the behavior for terms without namespaceSelector.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create namespaces ns-a and ns-c. ns-a has no labels initially.
2. Run pod worker in ns-a with labels app=worker.
3. Run pod scout in ns-c with this affinity:

```yaml
spec:
  affinity:
    podAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
      - labelSelector:
          matchLabels:
            app: worker
        namespaceSelector:
          matchLabels:
            team: one
        topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
```

scout stays Pending with FailedScheduling, for example `0/3 nodes are available: 3 node(s) didn't match pod affinity rules`.

4. Label the namespace: `kubectl label ns ns-a team=one`.
